title: The first keyboard instrument was an organ that used water to steady its air

cover.alt: A reconstructed Roman water organ on display: a wooden case topped by a row of metal pipes, with two long pump handles and a brass cylinder at the side.

body: The hydraulis, credited to Ctesibius of Alexandria, an engineer of the 3rd century BC, is the world’s earliest known keyboard instrument and the ancestor of the pipe organ. The water in it made no sound. Hand pumps pushed air into a reservoir with an open bottom standing in water, and the weight of the water kept pressing on that air, so the pressure stayed **steady** even though the pumping came in bursts. The instrument stayed in use across the Roman world through antiquity.

steps.label: Hand pumps push air in, in bursts
Air collects in a tank standing in water
The water presses back, evening out the air
Keys let the steady air into the pipes

slides.alt: A museum display: a glass case of corroded metal organ parts laid out flat on the left, and a reconstructed wooden organ with metal pipes on the right.
slides.caption: The Aquincum organ, found in Hungary in 1931: surviving metal parts on the left, and the working replica they made possible on the right.

slides.heading: Match the evidence to its date
slides.explanation: The Aquincum organ carries an inscription with its date. In 757 Emperor Constantine V sent a hydraulic organ to the Carolingian court.

slides.question: The first 19 of the Dion organ’s 24 pipes step down in height. How tall is the longest?
slides.explanation: 89 cm, stepping down to 22 cm. They are open pipes with a conical lower end, and their inner width shrinks from 2 to 1.5 cm.

slides.heading: Found at the foot of Olympus
slides.text: In 1992 archaeologists at Dion, an ancient Macedonian city near Mount Olympus in Greece, found the remains of a 1st-century BC organ. Its pipes survived, but the lower part with the air-pressing system was missing.
